Unfortunately, the pre-emptor without seeking any remedy before the higher Court subsequently filed an application under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for adding the left out co-sharers as parties in the pre-emption case. The Appellate Court rejected the said petition and the pre-emptor preferred Civil Revision No. 2969 of 2011 before the High Court Division and this Division was pleased to discharge the Rule and after that, the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal was filed before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division was also pleased to dismiss the same. 

 17. He finally submits that the findings of the Appellate Court as alast court of facts is based on evidence on record and there is no misreading, non reading and non-consideration of evidences on record and, as such, the same does not warrant for any interference by this Court; therefore, the Rule is liable to be turned down. 

 23. It appears from the record that the pre-emption case started its journey in the year, 1985. The pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-4 filed a written objection on 14-9-1987. In the written objection under paragraph Nos. 6 and 18, they contended that all the co-sharers of the holding were not made parties. The pre-emptor on 13-9-1988 filed an application for interrogatories requesting to supply the names and addresses of the co-sharers of the case holding. On 21-12-1988, the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-4 answered to the interrogatories without mentioning the names and addresses of any person and thereby the pre-emptees waived their right to defend that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties. The opposite party No. 4 along with the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-3 filed a joint written objection against the pre-emption case on 14-7-1987 and after that, the opposite No. 4, Rabeya Khatun, left this transitory world and after her sad demise, her legal heirs were substituted as opposite party Nos. 4(Ka)-4(Ga) by Order No. 142 dated 31-3-1997. The opposite party No. 4(Ka) entered appearance in the case and by filing another written objection on 11-9-1997 made specific averment therein that all the co-sharers in the khatian were not made parties. Since the pre-emptee No. 4, Rabeya khatun, waived her right to defend as to the issue of joinder of necessary parties. One of the substituted heirs of Rebaya Khatun i.e. the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 4(Ka), Kamal Uddin Khan's further written objection making specific averments to the effect that some persons were not made parties to the pre-emption case is an afterthought attempt to get the pre-emption application dismissed for defect of parties. The substituted legal heirs cannot fill up the lacuna of the original pre-emptee No. 4, Rabeya Khatun. It is a settled principle of law that all objections on the grounds of non-joinder of parties have to be taken at the earliest possible opportunity, if it is not taken shall be deemed, have been waived. It is true that non-joinder of necessary parties in pre-emption case is fatal. The pre-emptee-opposite party has to make clear averments in his pleadings i.e. the written objection that who are necessary parties. Mere general denial or gentleman denial in the written objection shall not if so facto dismiss the pre-emption case on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties. Since the pre-emptor requested to answer and gave the details of the persons, who are necessary parties, therefore, the defence of the pre-emptees has been struck out to that effect. The consequence of failure of giving answer to the interrogatories has been clearly spelt out under Order 11 Rule 21 of the CPC. In this respect, I am tempted to the ratio decided in the case reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 456 wherein the Apex Court held: 

 "A reference to Order 11, Rule 21 indicates that it is in two parts. The first part provides for the liability incurred by the defaulting party which fails to comply with any order to answer the interrogatories etc. and the other part prescribes the penalty for default, and it is that if the defaulting party is the plaintiff, penalty is the dismissal of the suit for, non-prosecution and if a defendant, his defence is to be struck off and be would be placed in the position as if he had not defended. The second part of the rule also provides for a procedure, for enforcing the penalty and it must be on an application of the interrogating party and on such application, the court assumes the jurisdiction to impose the penalty under the rule."
